merchant-cash-advance|restaurants-and-ho.h1: Merchant cash advance for restaurants and hospitality
merchant-cash-advance|restaurants-and-ho.title: Merchant Cash Advance for Restaurants | Loanleaf
merchant-cash-advance|restaurants-and-ho.desc: How a merchant cash advance works for UK restaurants, cafés, pubs and hotels, and what providers look at in your card takings. Free introduction to a broker.
merchant-cash-advance|restaurants-and-ho.lead: An advance repaid from a share of your card takings, so repayments follow the covers through busy weekends and quiet Tuesdays.
intro: A restaurant or pub can look very different to a lender depending on how its money comes in. A merchant cash advance is judged on your card terminal history rather than your assets, which suits venues where most diners pay by card. Providers usually want to see several months of card settlements, and many prefer six to twelve, so they can see how a typical week compares with a busy December or a flat February.

A share of each day’s card sales goes towards the advance until the agreed total is repaid. Cash takings, tips handled separately and delivery platform payouts that arrive in your bank account rather than through your own terminal usually do not count towards the card share. If a large part of your trade is cash or comes through delivery apps, the advance may be smaller than you expect, and a broker can explain how providers treat each stream.
uses: Winter shortfall
Cover rent, wages and supplier bills in January and February, when covers drop and the repayment share falls with them.
Pre-season stock and staff
Pay for extra stock and temporary staff before a summer terrace season or the Christmas party bookings, which land before the money does.
Unexpected repair
Replace a failed walk-in fridge or extraction fan quickly, where waiting for a longer application could mean closing for service.
Short refresh
Fund a smaller refresh such as new furniture, a menu relaunch or a licensing change without agreeing fixed monthly payments.
fit: Typical amounts

Providers often size an advance as a multiple of average monthly card takings, so a café with £25,000 a month on the terminal might be offered a few months’ worth, subject to the provider’s checks. Smaller sums are common, and you repay over a period that depends on sales rather than a fixed term.
How repayment lines up

Because the repayment share is taken from daily settlements, a weekend rush repays more than a wet Monday. That flexibility is the main reason hospitality owners consider this route, but it also means the advance clears faster in strong weeks, which affects the total cost.
What providers check

They look at card volumes, how steady the takings are across the year, and whether the terminal is held with a provider that can be linked to repayments. Switching terminal provider part way through usually needs the advance provider’s agreement, so check this before you do.
considerations: Cost against a standard loan

The cost is a fixed fee rather than annual interest, so a quick repayment in a busy summer can make the effective cost high. Ask for the total repayable and compare it with a fixed-term loan or asset finance for the same purpose.
Less cash coming in daily
A slice of every card sale is taken before it reaches your bank. If margins are already thin, check that what remains still covers food costs, wages and VAT, particularly in quiet weeks.
When it may not suit

If most sales are cash or delivery platform payouts, or if the need is a large one-off such as a full refurbishment, a fixed-term loan or a facility may fit better. A broker might point you towards those instead.
faqs: Do tips and service charge count towards the repayment share?

It depends on how your terminal and payroll handle them. Providers normally take their share from card settlements into your account, which may include service charge paid to the business but not tips distributed through a separate system. A broker can ask the provider how your setup would be treated before you commit.
What if my restaurant has a poor month?

The share is a percentage of card sales, so a poor month means a smaller repayment. The advance then takes longer to clear, though many agreements expect it to be repaid within a stated period, so ask what happens if takings fall well short of the plan.
Can I take a merchant cash advance if I mostly take bookings and cash?

It is harder. Providers focus on card volumes, so a venue with a large share of cash sales may be offered less. Some will consider overall bank turnover instead, and a broker can tell you which providers work that way.
Is there a personal guarantee?

Some providers ask directors for one, particularly on larger advances, while others rely on the card flow alone. Check the wording in the agreement, including what happens if the business closes or changes premises, before you sign. If the advance is small relative to your card volumes, some providers waive it, so it is worth asking.
Can I have a merchant cash advance and another loan?

Sometimes, but providers look at your existing commitments and may be less willing to lend if repayments are already stretched. Tell the broker about everything you owe so they can approach lenders likely to consider your full position. A broker can tell you which providers are comfortable with other debt sitting alongside theirs.

asset-finance|restaurants-and-hospitalit.h1: Asset finance for restaurants and hospitality
asset-finance|restaurants-and-hospitalit.title: Asset Finance for Restaurants and Hotels | Loanleaf
asset-finance|restaurants-and-hospitalit.desc: How asset finance works for UK restaurants, pubs, cafés and hotels buying kitchen equipment, coffee machines and fit-out items. Get matched with a broker.
asset-finance|restaurants-and-hospitalit.lead: Spread the cost of ovens, cold rooms and coffee machines across their working life, with the kit itself acting as security.
intro: A commercial kitchen is mostly equipment: ranges, combi ovens, blast chillers, dishwashers, extraction and refrigeration. These items cost thousands each, they are usually bought in a hurry when something fails, and they keep their value better than most venue spend. That makes them a natural fit for asset finance, where the lender buys the item and your company pays for it in instalments over a set period, typically matched to how long the equipment should last.

The finance is secured on the equipment, so lenders look first at what you are buying and whether it holds its resale value. New kit from a recognised supplier is straightforward to value. Bespoke joinery, decoration and installation labour are harder to finance because the lender could not easily resell them. Many venues therefore finance the equipment itself and fund the wider refurbishment from another source, which a broker can help structure.
uses: Replacing a failed fridge or oven
Get a like-for-like replacement installed quickly and spread the bill, rather than taking a large lump out of cash during a busy period.
New coffee and bar equipment
Finance a commercial espresso machine, glass washer or keg system, often supplied with a servicing arrangement from the supplier.
Equipping a new site
Buy the full kitchen package for a second venue and repay it from the new site’s takings, keeping the first site’s cash for running costs.
Energy-efficient upgrades
Swap ageing refrigeration or induction hobs for newer kit, where lower running costs help offset the monthly payment.
fit: Terms and amounts

Terms of two to five years are common, often shorter for items such as small appliances and longer for large fixed plant. A café buying a £12,000 coffee and kitchen package, for example, might repay it over around three years, subject to the lender’s checks. Deposits vary by lender and by how old the business is.
Hire purchase or lease

With hire purchase your company ends up owning the kit once payments finish. With leasing you often return or upgrade it, which suits fast-changing items such as coffee systems. Whichever you choose, the tax and VAT treatment differs, so check with your accountant.
What lenders check

They want the supplier’s quote, evidence the equipment will be used by the business and usually recent bank statements and accounts. Used equipment can often be financed, but the lender will consider its age and who is selling it. Weaker trading figures may mean a larger deposit.
considerations: Fixed instalments in a seasonal trade

Hospitality income moves across the year, but asset finance payments stay the same. Check the monthly figure is affordable in your quietest month, not only the average, and ask whether any lender allows seasonal or stepped payments.
Installation and fit-out costs

Lenders often finance equipment only, so ducting, plumbing, electrics and decoration may need another source. Ask the supplier to split the quote so the finance covers only the part that can act as security.
Equipment you may outgrow
If you expect to change concept or move premises, long terms can leave you paying for kit you no longer use. Leasing or a shorter term may suit better, and early settlement terms are worth checking.
faqs: Can I finance second-hand kitchen equipment?

Often, yes. Lenders will look at the age, make and condition, and whether you are buying from a dealer or a private seller. Dealers are usually easier. Terms may be shorter and a larger deposit may be asked for compared with new equipment.
Does asset finance cover installation?

Sometimes, when installation is part of the supplier’s invoice for the equipment. Building work, ventilation ductwork and decoration are less likely to be covered because they cannot easily be resold. A broker can explain how lenders have treated similar packages.
Will the equipment belong to me?

With hire purchase, yes, once the final payment is made, often after a small option fee. With a lease, the lender keeps ownership and you either return the kit, extend the lease or sometimes buy it at the end. Check which structure the offer uses.
Do I need to own the building?

No. Because the equipment is the security, many tenants and leaseholders use asset finance. Lenders may ask how long your lease has left, since removable kit in a short-lease premises is harder to recover. Lenders mainly want to be sure they could collect the equipment if payments stopped, so access to the kit matters more than who owns the building.
Is a personal guarantee needed?

It depends on the lender, the amount and the age of the company. Smaller deals on established limited companies sometimes proceed without one, while newer businesses or larger amounts may need directors to guarantee. The broker can tell you before you apply.

unsecured-business-loans|restaurants-and.h1: Unsecured business loans for restaurants and hospitality
unsecured-business-loans|restaurants-and.title: Unsecured Loans for Restaurants and Hospitality | Loanleaf
unsecured-business-loans|restaurants-and.desc: How unsecured business loans work for UK restaurants, cafés, pubs and hotels planning a refresh, a relaunch or a new site. Free match with a specialist broker.
unsecured-business-loans|restaurants-and.lead: A fixed sum for a refurbishment, relaunch or second site, repaid monthly without putting your premises or kit up as security.
intro: Many hospitality owners lease their premises and have little to offer as security beyond the equipment already in the building. An unsecured loan is judged on the company’s trading record instead: how long you have been open, how steady your takings are across the year and whether existing commitments leave room for a new repayment. For a restaurant that reopens each spring after a refresh, or a pub adding bedrooms, it can be a straightforward way to pay for the work in one go.

Because repayments are fixed, the shape of your year matters. A venue that earns most of its income between May and September has to find the same payment in February. Lenders will usually ask for twelve months of bank statements so they can see how the quiet spells are handled. A broker can use this to suggest a term and amount that the whole year can support, rather than just the strongest quarter.
uses: Refurbishing the dining room
Redo seating, flooring and lighting during a planned closure, paying the contractor on completion rather than from the till.
Adding rooms or a terrace
Build out outdoor space or convert upstairs rooms to add covers or bedrooms, with the extra income expected to cover repayments.
Relaunching a concept
Rebrand, retrain staff and buy a new menu’s worth of stock when a venue changes style, without selling any equipment.
Opening a second venue
Pay for the deposit, fit-out and early wages for a new site while the original business keeps trading.
fit: Amounts and terms

Amounts from £5,000 up to several hundred thousand are possible, depending mainly on turnover and affordability. A restaurant with £600,000 a year in sales might, for example, look at a loan of £40,000 to £60,000 over two to four years, subject to lender checks. Longer terms lower the monthly payment but increase the total interest.
Matching term to the project

A refurbishment that refreshes the venue for five years can reasonably be paid back over three to five. A one-off marketing push or stock build is better matched to a shorter term. Overborrowing for a short-lived benefit leaves repayments running long after the benefit has gone.
What lenders check

Bank statements, filed accounts and existing borrowing, plus a credit search on the company and usually on the directors. Strong card takings, steady margins and no recent missed payments help. A lease with little time left can lead some lenders to reduce the amount or pass.
considerations: Personal guarantees
Most lenders ask directors to guarantee unsecured loans personally. For an owner-operator whose home is their main asset, understand what the guarantee could mean if the venue struggles.
Fixed payments in quiet months
If takings fall sharply in winter, a fixed payment can strain cash. Work out the lowest monthly takings in the past year and check the payment still fits, with room for VAT and rent.
Cost and fees

Unsecured loans can cost more than borrowing against property or equipment. Compare the total repayable, and check for arrangement fees and early repayment charges. If the main purchase is equipment, asset finance may cost less.
faqs: Can a venue on a short lease get an unsecured loan?

Sometimes. Lenders mainly look at trading, but a lease with only a year or two left can reduce the amount offered or the term available. If you are about to renew, mention it to the broker early, since a signed extension can help.
How quickly can a loan be arranged?

Timescales vary by lender and by how soon you provide documents. Some decisions come within days, others take longer for larger sums. Having twelve months of statements and your latest accounts ready usually helps. If the work has a fixed start date, such as a planned closure, start the application well before it.
Does the loan have to be for a specific purpose?

Unsecured loans are generally flexible, though lenders may ask what the money is for. A clear plan, such as a refurbishment with quotes, can help show that the repayment is affordable. Quotes from contractors and a rough timetable are the documents most often requested.
Can I borrow for a venue that’s been open less than a year?

Loanleaf works with companies trading for six months or more with revenue of £50,000 or above. Within that, some lenders want a longer history, so a broker can say which are likely to consider a younger venue. A longer record, ideally including one full winter, widens the choice of lenders.
What if I already have a merchant cash advance?

Existing advances count as commitments, and some lenders will not lend alongside one. Tell the broker about it at the start. It may affect the options or the amount available. Some lenders will still consider the application if the advance is small or nearly repaid, so give the broker the balance and expected end date.

commercial-mortgages|restaurants-and-hos.h1: Commercial mortgages for restaurants and hospitality
commercial-mortgages|restaurants-and-hos.title: Commercial Mortgages for Pubs and Restaurants | Loanleaf
commercial-mortgages|restaurants-and-hos.desc: How commercial mortgages work for UK pubs, restaurants, hotels and cafés buying or refinancing their premises. Free introduction to a specialist finance broker.
commercial-mortgages|restaurants-and-hos.lead: Long-term finance to buy or refinance a pub, restaurant or hotel, valued partly on what the business earns as well as the building.
intro: A hospitality property is valued differently from an office or a warehouse. Lenders often consider the trading business as well as the bricks, because a licensed pub or hotel is worth more as a going concern than as an empty building. They usually ask for several years of accounts, so they can judge a level of profit the venue can reasonably be expected to keep making, and the valuer may use that figure alongside the property’s own value.

For an owner-occupier buying their freehold, this can mean repayments that sit close to the rent they pay now, which is the reason many operators consider it. Typical commercial mortgages run from ten to twenty-five years, often with a deposit of 25% to 40% of the price, depending on the lender and the property. Licensing, planning use class and the condition of the building all feed into the lender’s decision, so a broker who knows the sector can save time.
uses: Buying your freehold
Purchase the pub or restaurant you currently rent, so repayments build equity in the building rather than going to a landlord.
Acquiring a going concern
Buy an existing licensed venue, including the goodwill, fixtures and licence, with the lender considering its trading history.
Refinancing existing debt
Replace a short-term or higher-cost loan on the premises with a longer-term arrangement that has more manageable repayments.
Releasing equity for investment
Borrow against a premises you own to pay for an extension, extra bedrooms or a second site, rather than using unsecured borrowing.
fit: Amounts and deposits

Loan-to-value for hospitality property is often lower than for standard commercial property, with many lenders offering around 60% to 75% of the valuation, subject to affordability. A £600,000 freehold might therefore need a deposit of £150,000 or more, plus legal and valuation costs.
How trading is assessed

Lenders usually want to see profits sufficient to cover repayments with a margin to spare. They often ask for two or three years of accounts, and may look at whether the existing management is staying on. A new operator buying a venue may find the options are narrower.
Property specifics

A pub with a tied agreement, a hotel with rooms above, or a restaurant with flats overhead may be valued and financed differently. Planning, licence conditions and the state of repair can all matter, so have surveys and licensing documents ready.
considerations: Time and cost to arrange
Commercial mortgages involve valuations, searches and legal work, so they take longer than other business finance. Budget for valuation, legal and arrangement fees on top of the deposit.
Long commitment, uncertain trade

Hospitality income can swing with the economy, so a twenty-year term needs a margin of safety. Consider whether repayments would still be affordable in a poor year and whether rates are fixed or variable.
When another route may be better

If you need a smaller sum quickly, or the premises are leased, a loan or asset finance may be more suitable. If you want to buy at auction, a bridging loan may be raised first and refinanced onto a mortgage afterwards.
faqs: Can I get a commercial mortgage on a leasehold pub?

Generally not, as the lender needs security over the property itself. If you only hold a long lease, some lenders may consider it, depending on the length remaining. A broker can explain what has been accepted for leaseholds in your situation.
Does the licence need to be in my company’s name?

Lenders will want the premises licence and the designated premises supervisor to be properly in place. The detail depends on the venue. Your solicitor and the broker can confirm what a lender is likely to want before you commit. Late changes to the licence holder or supervisor can delay completion, so sort these early.
How much deposit will I need?

Commonly between 25% and 40% of the purchase price, though it varies by lender, property and your trading record. Costs such as valuation, legal fees and any arrangement fee are usually on top of the deposit. A strong trading record, a lower price or extra security can sometimes reduce the amount asked.
Is a hotel treated differently from a restaurant?

Often, yes. Hotels are valued on room income and occupancy as well as property value, so lenders look at accounts in detail. A restaurant with a long track record and clear profit can be easier than a newer hotel with variable occupancy.
Can I use a commercial mortgage to buy a new site while keeping my first venue?

Possibly, though lenders will consider your combined borrowing and trading across both sites. Some will want security over existing properties. A broker can assess how a second purchase fits alongside the first. Expect them to ask for management accounts for both sites and a plan for how the new venue will trade.

revolving-credit-facility|restaurants-an.h1: Revolving credit facility for restaurants and hospitality
revolving-credit-facility|restaurants-an.title: Revolving Credit for Restaurants and Hospitality | Loanleaf
revolving-credit-facility|restaurants-an.desc: How a revolving credit facility helps UK restaurants, pubs and hotels smooth supplier bills, wages and seasonal dips. Free match with a specialist broker.
revolving-credit-facility|restaurants-an.lead: A credit limit you draw on when a bill lands and repay when the takings arrive, with interest only on what you use.
intro: Hospitality cash flow is lumpy in small, repeated ways. Suppliers want payment within days, wages go out weekly or monthly, rent and VAT fall due on fixed dates, and takings rise and fall with the weather. A revolving credit facility is a limit agreed in advance, which the company draws on as needed and pays back as money comes in. Once repaid, the headroom is available again, so one facility can cover many small gaps through the year.

Because you pay interest only on the amount drawn, a facility can be cheaper than a loan for short, recurring needs, though most lenders also charge an arrangement fee and may review the limit each year. They usually ask for twelve months of bank statements and may take a charge over company assets or a director’s guarantee. A broker can explain which lenders prefer to work with hospitality businesses and how they set the limit.
uses: Bridging the winter
Draw on the facility to pay wages and suppliers in January and February, and repay it through spring as bookings recover.
Stocking up for peak periods
Buy wine, spirits and food ahead of Christmas or a bank holiday weekend, clearing the balance with the takings that follow.
Waiting for event payments
Cover staffing and food for a wedding or corporate event where the customer pays a balance after the date.
Smoothing VAT and rent
Pay a quarterly VAT or rent bill on time, then repay from the following weeks’ trade rather than disturbing day-to-day cash.
fit: Setting the limit

Lenders often base the limit on turnover and the pattern of your bank account, and a venue turning over £800,000 a year might be offered a limit in the tens of thousands, subject to the lender’s checks. It is usually sensible to ask for a limit that covers your regular peak shortfall rather than the maximum on offer.
How it differs from an overdraft

A facility is typically a separate agreement with its own limit and terms, not tied to your current account. Some are committed for a year or more, which means the lender cannot simply withdraw the headroom. Others are uncommitted and can be reviewed more freely, so ask which kind it is.
What lenders look at

They check that the account moves in a healthy way, with money coming in regularly and the facility being repaid, not sitting permanently at its limit. A facility used as a permanent loan can lead to a poor review, so plan repayments rather than letting the balance linger.
considerations: Variable cost
Interest is often variable and charged on daily balances, with fees for arranging, renewing or not using the facility. Add up the likely cost over a year against a fixed-term loan before deciding.
Not for long-term investment
A facility suits short, repeating gaps. Using it to pay for a refurbishment that will take years to earn back is risky, because the lender could reduce or end the limit when you still owe the money.
Security and guarantees

Lenders may take security over company assets or ask directors for personal guarantees. If the venue struggles, those arrangements can bite quickly, so read the terms closely and keep your repayment plan realistic.
faqs: Is a revolving credit facility the same as an overdraft?

They are similar in feel, but a facility is usually a separate agreement with its own limit, terms and fees, and may not be tied to your current account. Ask the broker how any facility on offer differs from your existing bank arrangements.
Can I draw on it at short notice?

Often yes, once it is set up. Many facilities let you draw through an online portal or a phone call, with funds arriving within a day or so. Check how long it takes and whether there are minimum draw amounts.
What happens if I leave it fully drawn for months?

Lenders may see this as a sign the business needs a loan instead, and could reduce the limit at review. If your need is permanent rather than seasonal, a fixed-term loan may be more appropriate. A shorter-term repayment plan agreed up front can keep the facility healthy.
How long does the facility last?

Terms vary, with many reviewed or renewed annually and some committed for longer. At renewal, the lender looks again at your accounts and may change the limit or price. A broker can find out how a lender treats renewals. Ask whether the limit is committed for the term or can be withdrawn on review, as this affects how much you can rely on it.
Will it work if I run several venues?

Possibly. Lenders may look at the company holding the sites or the group. Having separate companies can complicate things, so tell the broker how your venues are structured when you apply. Some lenders can cover a group through one facility, which can be simpler than managing several.

vat-and-tax-loans|restaurants-and-hospit.h1: VAT and tax loans for restaurants and hospitality
vat-and-tax-loans|restaurants-and-hospit.title: VAT and Tax Loans for Restaurants and Hotels | Loanleaf
vat-and-tax-loans|restaurants-and-hospit.desc: How VAT and tax loans work for UK restaurants, pubs and hotels facing a quarterly VAT bill after a quiet spell. Free match with a specialist finance broker.
vat-and-tax-loans|restaurants-and-hospit.lead: Spread a VAT, PAYE or corporation tax bill over a few months when it lands just after your quietest weeks.
intro: VAT is charged on most restaurant and hotel sales, and the quarterly bill reflects everything the venue took in over three months, whether or not that money is still in the bank. The awkward case is a quarter that ends after a busy December: the bill is large because takings were high, but January and February cash is thin. Wages, rent and suppliers keep going, so the VAT payment competes with everything else. A tax loan lets the company pay HMRC on time and repay the lender in instalments.

Because the loan covers a known bill, lenders can assess it more simply than a general loan. They check that the company is profitable overall, that its returns are filed and that it is not already behind with HMRC. A broker will often ask for your latest VAT return, which shows the amount and the due date, and a few months of bank statements so the lender can see whether the repayments sit comfortably.
uses: VAT after the festive quarter
Pay the VAT due in early February out of a Christmas-heavy quarter without draining the January cash needed for wages and supplier bills.
PAYE and National Insurance
Cover a monthly payroll tax payment during a short dip, particularly in venues with a large seasonal workforce.
Corporation tax after a strong year
Settle a corporation tax bill in full where the year’s profit has been reinvested in a refurbishment or new kit.
Catching up after a repair
Replace cash used on an urgent equipment failure, so the tax bill is paid on time rather than late.
fit: Amounts and terms

Tax loans typically run for three to twelve months, so repayments are relatively high compared with the length of the loan. A venue facing a £30,000 VAT bill might, for example, spread it over six months, subject to lender checks, and need to budget for the monthly figure plus any fee.
Compared with Time to Pay

HMRC can sometimes agree a Time to Pay arrangement for a tax bill, with its own interest charged on the balance. A loan is a separate commercial agreement. It can be quicker and avoids a payment plan with HMRC, but usually carries lender fees, so compare the full cost.
What lenders check

Profitability, VAT returns filed on time and no existing arrears are the main points. Lenders also look at the bank statements for signs of stress. Having the VAT return and due date to hand helps the broker approach the right lenders.
considerations: It spreads the bill, it does not remove it
A tax loan only moves the cost across months. If margins are thin, make sure the extra repayment does not push you into the same problem next quarter, and set money aside for the next VAT bill.
Leave time before the deadline

Lenders need days or weeks to assess an application. Starting only a few days before the due date risks a late payment, which brings HMRC penalties and interest, so approach a broker as soon as you see the shortfall.
Recurring problems

If VAT regularly causes pressure, a better fix may be a separate savings account or a different VAT scheme, which an accountant can advise on. A broker might also suggest a revolving facility if the shortfall repeats.
faqs: Can I get a tax loan if I already owe HMRC?

Options are narrower. Many lenders prefer companies that are up to date, though some will consider those with a Time to Pay arrangement in place. A broker can explain which lenders might look at your situation. Being open about the arrears and the repayment plan generally helps the conversation.
Does the lender pay HMRC directly?

Some do, and some pay the money to your business so you can settle the bill. Either way, make sure the payment reaches HMRC by the deadline, and keep the reference number of the payment. Keep the payment confirmation, as HMRC may take a few days to allocate the money to your account.
Is a tax loan cheaper than late payment?

Late payment brings penalties and interest from HMRC, which can build up. A loan has its own interest and fees, so compare the two. Often the loan costs less than penalties, but the answer depends on the terms and how late you would be.
What can I use the loan for?

Lenders typically specify a VAT, PAYE or corporation tax bill and may want to see the demand or return. This is different from a general loan, which could be used for anything but may cost more. Check the terms if you also want to cover other costs, since extra borrowing may need a separate product.
How is a hospitality business viewed for this?

Lenders understand that takings and VAT follow the season. A venue with a clear seasonal pattern, steady profit and returns filed on time is usually easier to assess than one with irregular figures. A broker can help explain any unusual quarter, such as a large event or a closure, so the lender sees the full picture.

secured-business-loans|restaurants-and-h.h1: Secured business loans for restaurants and hospitality
secured-business-loans|restaurants-and-h.title: Secured Business Loans for Restaurants and Hotels | Loanleaf
secured-business-loans|restaurants-and-h.desc: How secured business loans work for UK restaurants, pubs and hotels borrowing against property for a larger refurbishment or a second site. Free broker match.
secured-business-loans|restaurants-and-h.lead: Borrow a larger sum over a longer term by putting property behind the loan, for projects an unsecured lender would not fund alone.
intro: Some hospitality projects cost more than a trading record alone will support: a full gut refurbishment, converting an upper floor into letting rooms, or taking on a second and third site. A secured loan lets the company offer a charge over property, usually premises the business or its directors own, so the lender has something to rely on if repayments stop. In return, lenders tend to offer larger amounts, longer terms and a lower cost than unsecured borrowing.

The security does not have to be the venue itself. A pub owner might offer a different freehold, or a director may offer a buy-to-let property, and lenders will take a first or second charge depending on what is already borrowed. The valuation and the existing debt decide how much is available, so the amount may be quite different from what the trading figures would suggest. A broker can explain how each lender values licensed property.
uses: Converting upper floors
Turn unused space above a pub or restaurant into letting rooms, paying contractors over a term that matches the years the rooms will earn.
Major refurbishment
Fund a full refit of a hotel wing or restaurant, where costs run well beyond what an unsecured lender is likely to offer.
Expanding to more sites
Raise money for several openings over a period, using a property charge to support a larger overall amount.
Consolidating borrowing
Replace several merchant advances, loans and facilities with one repayment, which can ease monthly cash flow.
fit: Amounts and terms

Amounts can run from tens of thousands to well over £1m, depending on the value of the security and how much is already borrowed on it. Terms of five to twenty years are possible. As an example, a charge over a £900,000 freehold with £400,000 outstanding might support a further £100,000 or so, subject to the lender’s checks.
First or second charge

A first charge means the lender is first in line if things go wrong, which usually costs less. A second charge sits behind an existing mortgage and may need the first lender’s consent. A broker can say which route is realistic for your property.
What lenders check

A valuation of the property, the company’s trading and affordability, and the credit of the company and directors. Legal work follows, so allow several weeks. For licensed premises, lenders will often also consider the going-concern value of the trade.
considerations: The security is at risk

If repayments cannot be met, the lender can enforce against the property. Where the charge is over a director’s own property, that can include their home or investment, so take independent legal advice before agreeing.
Costs and time
Valuation, legal fees and arrangement fees add to the cost, and the process takes longer than unsecured lending. Weigh this against the saving in interest and the larger amount.
Longer terms, more interest
A long term lowers the monthly payment but increases the total interest. Match the term to how long the improvement will earn, and check whether overpayments or early repayment are allowed.
faqs: Can I use my home as security for a business loan?

Some lenders will accept a director’s residential property as security, but the risk is yours personally. Take legal advice first, and ask a broker whether alternatives such as business property or equipment could be used instead. Lenders may also ask for a spouse or co-owner’s consent, which adds time to the process.
What is the difference from a commercial mortgage?

A commercial mortgage is usually used to buy or refinance a specific property. A secured loan may be used for a wider purpose and secured on any suitable property. The line is blurry, and a broker can say which best fits your plan.
Will a second charge be accepted?

Often, depending on the existing lender’s terms and the property’s value. A second charge usually costs more than a first, since the lender is behind existing debt. The first lender’s consent may be needed. Having the existing lender’s consent in hand early avoids delays at completion.
How long does a secured loan take?

Longer than unsecured. A valuation, legal checks and title work are involved, so several weeks is common, and longer for complex properties. Preparing documents such as accounts and title details early can help. Complex titles, planning issues or several owners add further time, so allow for that in any plans.
Can I borrow if the venue is leased?

You need some property to offer. If you rent your venue, a secured loan would need to be backed by another property, such as one a director owns. Otherwise asset finance or an unsecured loan may suit better. If you hold a long lease, ask the broker, as a small number of lenders will consider it in some cases.

asset-finance|construction-and-trades.h1: Asset finance for construction and trades
asset-finance|construction-and-trades.title: Asset Finance for Construction and Trades | Loanleaf
asset-finance|construction-and-trades.desc: How asset finance works for UK builders, groundworkers and trade firms buying vans, excavators and plant. Free introduction to a specialist finance broker.
asset-finance|construction-and-trades.lead: Spread the cost of vans, excavators and tools across their working life, with the machine itself acting as security.
intro: Trades run on kit. A groundworks firm needs diggers and dumpers, an electrician needs a fleet of vans with racking, a scaffolder needs a lorry and thousands of tube and fittings. These items cost tens of thousands each and hold their value reasonably well, so asset finance fits: the lender buys the equipment, your company pays monthly, and the asset is the security. This often means a business can get kit without a large deposit or a charge over property.

Lenders value construction equipment carefully because machines vary a great deal. A three-year-old excavator from a main dealer with a service history is easy to price. A heavily used machine, an unusual attachment or something bought privately is harder. Vehicles carry their own checks, such as age and mileage. Because of this, lenders ask for a detailed quote or invoice and may adjust the deposit, the term or the rate to reflect resale risk.
uses: Replacing a tired excavator
Swap a machine with rising repair bills for a newer one, spreading the payments over the years you expect to use it.
Adding vans for a growing team
Finance several vehicles at once as you take on apprentices or a second crew, rather than paying for each one up front.
Specialist tools and attachments
Buy breakers, laser levels, scaffolding systems or access platforms that a job needs, where hire costs are adding up.
Buying plant instead of hiring
Move from regular hire to ownership when a machine is on site most of the year and hire invoices exceed the monthly payment.
fit: Terms and amounts

Terms of two to five years are common for plant and vehicles, with the term usually kept shorter than the machine’s expected life. A groundworks firm financing a £55,000 used excavator might, for example, spread payments over four years, subject to the lender’s checks. Deposits and rates depend on the age of the kit and the age of the company.
Hire purchase or lease

Hire purchase leads to ownership once paid, which suits machines you will run for a decade. Leasing and contract hire can keep monthly costs lower and suit vehicles you will replace regularly. VAT and capital allowance treatment differs, so speak to your accountant.
What lenders check

Supplier quotes, the age and make of the asset, and your bank statements and accounts. Lenders will also look at your order book and how you plan to use the kit. Used plant from a dealer is generally easier than from a private seller.
considerations: Machine downtime and work gaps

Payments continue even when a job falls through or the weather stops work. Check the monthly figure is affordable in a quiet month, and consider how much work the machine needs to earn to cover itself.
Resale value and condition

If a machine has been heavily used, or becomes obsolete as emissions rules change, its worth at the end may be lower than the lender expected. Keep service records, and ask what condition the lender requires on return.
Insurance and maintenance
The lender usually requires comprehensive insurance, and you remain responsible for upkeep. Include insurance, servicing and tracking in your cost calculation, not just the finance payment.
faqs: Can I finance second-hand plant?

Often, yes. Lenders look at age, make, hours and the seller. Dealer machines are usually easier to finance than private sales, and older equipment may have shorter terms or larger deposits. A service history and proof of ownership from the seller make a real difference to the lender’s view.
Will I need a deposit?

Not always. Some lenders offer finance for the full price of an asset for an established company, while others ask for a deposit, particularly for older equipment or younger businesses. A broker can say what is realistic for your situation.
Can I finance a van and a digger together?

Yes, lenders can combine several assets into one agreement, though some prefer separate agreements by asset type. Combining can simplify paperwork, but separating gives flexibility to settle one early. A single supplier invoice covering both assets is usually easier to process than two separate sellers.
What happens if I want to sell the machine early?

You usually need to settle the outstanding balance, and may pay an early settlement charge. With hire purchase, the lender has a claim on the asset until you do, so you cannot sell without clearing the agreement. Ask the lender for a settlement figure before you agree a sale, so you know what the buyer’s money must cover.
Do I need a personal guarantee?

Sometimes. Where the lender relies on the asset and the company’s history, a guarantee may not be needed, but newer companies and larger amounts often involve one. Ask the broker before you apply. Directors’ credit history is usually still checked, whether or not a guarantee is asked for.

invoice-finance|construction-and-trades.h1: Invoice finance for construction and trades
invoice-finance|construction-and-trades.title: Invoice Finance for Construction and Trades | Loanleaf
invoice-finance|construction-and-trades.desc: How invoice finance works for UK contractors and trade firms paid in arrears, including applications for payment and retentions. Free broker introduction.
invoice-finance|construction-and-trades.lead: Release cash tied up in certified work while you wait for the main contractor to pay, with provisions for retentions and stage payments.
intro: Construction invoicing is more complicated than a standard sale. Work is often paid through interim applications, a valuation is certified by the main contractor, and the final invoice comes weeks later. Retentions of 3% to 5% are held back for a year or more, and payment may be conditional on the main contractor being paid by the client. Standard invoice finance is built for simple invoices, so some providers are cautious about construction and others have specialist teams.

Where it works, invoice finance advances a large part of an approved invoice soon after it is issued, then pays the balance, less fees, when your customer pays. Lenders assess your customers’ credit more than your own, so a subcontractor working for a well-rated main contractor may qualify more easily than the size of the business suggests. A broker who knows the sector can point to providers who understand stage payments and retentions.
uses: Waiting on main contractor payments
Release cash on certified applications for payment so wages, materials and subcontractors can be paid before the 45-day wait.
Supporting a growing order book
Take on more work from existing customers without running short of cash, since the finance grows as invoicing grows.
Covering CIS and payroll weeks
Smooth the timing between weekly labour costs and monthly payment cycles on larger projects.
Using one facility across several jobs
Apply finance only to selected invoices from specific customers, so you are not tied to financing your whole turnover.
fit: Advance rates and what is excluded

Providers typically advance a high percentage of eligible invoices, with the balance paid when the customer settles. Retentions, disputed amounts and work not yet certified are normally excluded or treated separately, so the amount you can draw is often smaller than your total invoicing.
Selective or whole turnover

Selective facilities let you finance chosen invoices and suit firms with a few large customers. Whole-ledger facilities cover all invoices and may cost less, but tie you in. For a firm that bills one main contractor heavily, a selective facility may be the easier fit.
What providers check

Customer credit quality, how long they take to pay, contract terms and any history of disputes. They want to see applications and certificates, not just invoices. A construction firm with clean paperwork and creditworthy customers is usually easier to place.
considerations: Retentions and pay-when-paid terms
Retentions remain tied up for months, and pay-when-paid clauses can delay settlement. Check how the provider treats these and whether the facility funds only the net amount, not the full invoice.
Customer knowledge

Some arrangements notify your customers that a lender is involved, while confidential facilities do not. Think about how your main contractor might react, and ask which arrangement the provider offers.
Costs and minimums

Fees are made up of a service charge and a discount charge, and may include minimum annual fees. Add these up against the benefit of faster cash, and compare with an unsecured loan or a revolving facility.
faqs: Can I finance invoices that include retentions?

Usually the retention amount is excluded until it is released, though some providers can advance against retentions later or against invoices after practical completion. Ask the provider how it treats them. Some providers will also advance against an approved retention release, once the customer has confirmed it in writing.
Does the domestic reverse charge for VAT affect invoice finance?

It changes how VAT is shown on some construction invoices, since the customer accounts for the VAT. Providers who work in construction are used to this, and a broker can point you to those who are. Ask the provider how it handles invoices where VAT is not shown, so the advance is calculated on the correct amount.
Can I finance only one customer’s invoices?

Often yes, through a selective facility. This suits firms who are comfortable with the credit of one customer and prefer not to finance the rest. Fees may be slightly higher per invoice. Providers may set a minimum number or value of invoices each month, so ask what is expected.
What if my customer disputes an invoice?

Disputed invoices are generally excluded, or may have to be repaid to the lender if already advanced. Keep records of valuations, variations and approvals so disputes are minimal. A clear audit trail of applications, valuations and approvals makes disputes shorter and easier to resolve.
How long does set-up take?

Providers need to review your ledger, customers and contracts, and run credit checks, so a few weeks is common. Having a debtor list, recent accounts and sample invoices ready will help. Providers may also visit or phone your customers to verify invoices, so let your main contacts know it is coming.

unsecured-business-loans|construction-an.h1: Unsecured business loans for construction and trades
unsecured-business-loans|construction-an.title: Unsecured Business Loans for Construction | Loanleaf
unsecured-business-loans|construction-an.desc: How unsecured business loans work for UK builders and trade firms paying for materials, wages and mobilisation on a larger contract. Free broker match.
unsecured-business-loans|construction-an.lead: A fixed sum to mobilise a larger contract, paid for before the first stage payment and repaid in regular instalments.
intro: Winning a bigger contract can be a cash problem before it is a profit. The first weeks need materials ordered, subcontractors booked, extra labour on payroll and plant on site, and the first stage payment may be a month or more away. An unsecured loan gives the company a defined sum for that upfront cost, without a charge over a property or a machine. The lender looks at the company’s trading record and at whether the new contract is likely to make the repayments affordable.

The repayment term should follow the contract, not just the headline figure. A loan taken for a six-month fit-out is better matched to a 12-month term than a five-year one that outlasts the work. Lenders will often ask for evidence such as the signed contract, the payment schedule and the customer’s identity, because it shows where the repayments will come from. A broker can help present that evidence in the way lenders prefer.
uses: Mobilising a new contract
Order materials, hire plant and put extra labour on site before the first valuation is paid.
Hiring a second crew
Pay for a team’s wages and equipment during the weeks before the new work generates its own invoices.
Bridging a slow-paying customer
Cover running costs while a large invoice is delayed, repaying the loan once the customer settles.
Fit-out of a yard or workshop
Pay for racking, security, storage or a better office for the business, rather than renting or improvising.
fit: Amounts and terms

Unsecured loans for trade firms often range from £10,000 to £250,000 or more, depending on turnover and profit. A roofing contractor with £700,000 of annual turnover, for example, might consider around £50,000 over two years, subject to lender checks. Shorter terms suit contract-specific needs, longer ones suit permanent investment.
Using the contract as evidence

A signed contract with a creditworthy customer, a stage-payment schedule and a clear budget show lenders where the repayments will come from. This can matter more than a thin trading history, particularly for firms growing fast.
What lenders check

Bank statements, accounts, existing commitments, directors’ credit and, for larger sums, management accounts. Construction firms with seasonal winter dips or lumpy income should expect questions about how repayments would be met in a slow month.
considerations: Repayments start before the payment arrives
Instalments begin soon after the loan is paid out, whether or not the customer pays on time. Build in time for approvals and possible disputes when you plan the term.
Personal guarantees
Directors are normally asked to guarantee unsecured loans. For a sole-director limited company, that can put personal assets at risk if a contract goes badly.
Cost compared with secured options

Unsecured loans often cost more than asset finance or secured loans. If the need is mostly machinery, asset finance may be cheaper, and if cash is the problem on certified invoices, invoice finance could be a better fit.
faqs: Can I borrow to start a specific contract?

Yes, and lenders often like a clear purpose. Provide the contract, programme and payment terms so the broker can show how the loan will be repaid from the contract income. If the contract is subject to final approval, tell the broker, since some lenders will wait for a signed contract.
Will a loan be affected by winter slowdowns?

Lenders know construction is seasonal. They will look at how the business handled previous winters, so twelve months of bank statements that show this are useful. A fixed repayment must still be affordable in the quietest months. Showing a plan for covering winter, such as booked indoor work, helps lenders feel confident.
Can I get a loan without a long trading record?

Loanleaf works with companies trading for at least six months and with revenue of £50,000 or more. Some lenders ask for more history, so a broker can say which are most likely to consider a younger firm. A strong order book can help offset a short history in some lenders’ eyes.
What if my main customer pays late?

The loan repayment is still due. If this is a risk, a shorter term with a smaller payment, or invoice finance as a complement, might be more suitable. Discuss this with the broker. It also helps to have a cash buffer or a facility in reserve for when a payment slips.
Is a CIS deduction a problem for lenders?

No, it is a common feature of construction accounts. Lenders will look at net receipts, and CIS deductions are recoverable against your tax. Make sure your statements and accounts are up to date so the position is clear. If CIS is deducted from most of your invoices, say so, as it affects how cash comes into the business.

revolving-credit-facility|construction-a.h1: Revolving credit facility for construction and trades
revolving-credit-facility|construction-a.title: Revolving Credit for Construction and Trades | Loanleaf
revolving-credit-facility|construction-a.desc: How a revolving credit facility helps UK builders and trades manage materials, wages and weather delays between stage payments. Free broker introduction.
revolving-credit-facility|construction-a.lead: A standing credit limit for materials and wages, drawn when a job needs it and repaid when the stage payment lands.
intro: A building firm’s cash need changes with every job. In one month it may be ordering a roof structure, in the next paying subcontractors, and in a wet January it may be paying staff with little work on site. A revolving credit facility gives a limit that can be drawn on as needed and repaid as certificates are paid, so the same headroom serves many jobs through the year. Interest is charged only on the amount used, for as long as it is used.

For trades, this can suit a firm with regular, similar-sized jobs, as the facility is drawn at the start of each and cleared at the end. It is less suited to a business with one huge project that ties up cash for a year. Lenders will ask for twelve months of statements and may want to see the pattern of drawing and repaying. A broker can say which lenders accept construction business and which of them may want security.
uses: Paying merchants on time
Settle builders’ merchant bills in time to keep trade discounts, then repay from the next stage payment.
Weather and winter gaps
Cover wages and overheads when frost or rain stops outdoor work for a few weeks.
Overlapping jobs
Fund the start of a new job while another is waiting for final account and retention payments.
Small urgent costs
Pay for a replacement tool, a hire machine or a repair without taking out a fresh loan each time.
fit: Setting a sensible limit

Lenders set limits from turnover and cash flow, and a firm turning over £1m might be offered a limit in the tens of thousands, subject to checks. A sensible limit covers the largest regular materials bill plus a margin, not the largest amount available.
Drawing and repaying rhythm

Facilities work best when the balance goes up and down. If stage payments take 45 days, expect the balance to stay drawn for at least that long, and make sure the limit covers overlapping jobs without hitting the ceiling.
Security and review

Some facilities are secured on company assets or a debenture, others rely on director guarantees. Limits are reviewed, often yearly, and a firm that keeps a balance at its limit can expect a harder conversation at renewal.
considerations: Late payments drag the balance
If a main contractor holds back payment, the facility stays drawn and the interest runs. Keep a record of when each customer pays and size the limit with the slowest payer in mind.
Not a substitute for working capital
A facility that is always full is a sign the business is under-funded. If your need never clears, a fixed-term loan, invoice finance or a change in payment terms may fit better.
Variable costs and fees
Interest, arrangement fees and sometimes non-utilisation fees all add up. Compare the all-in cost of a year’s use with other options, particularly if you will draw on it for long periods.
faqs: Is a facility better than an overdraft for a builder?

It can be, because the limit is a separate agreement and may be harder for the lender to withdraw. Overdrafts are simpler but can be cut back when the bank reviews. A broker can compare the two for your firm.
Can I use it for CIS payments?

The facility is generally flexible and can be used for operating costs including subcontractor payments. Check the terms, as some lenders restrict use or ask about purpose. If you intend to use it for specific costs, such as tax payments or subcontractors, it is worth stating this when you apply.
What if I have several jobs overlapping?

That is where a facility earns its keep, since you can draw for the new job while the previous one is still unpaid. The lender will still look at your overall exposure, so keep your order book and invoice records clear.
Do lenders want security?

Often. Some lenders take a debenture over company assets, others ask for a director’s guarantee, and a few offer unsecured limits to strong businesses. The broker can explain the options for your size and history. Having a fully paid-off plant or a clean property to offer can open up better terms.
How quickly can I draw on it?

Once set up, drawdowns are usually quick, sometimes the same day. Setting up the facility itself takes longer as the lender reviews your accounts, statements and security. Ask about cut-off times and any fee per drawdown, since small charges can add up if you draw often.

secured-business-loans|construction-and-.h1: Secured business loans for construction and trades
secured-business-loans|construction-and-.title: Secured Business Loans for Construction | Loanleaf
secured-business-loans|construction-and-.desc: How secured business loans work for UK builders and contractors borrowing against property for a yard, a bigger contract or a purchase. Free broker match.
secured-business-loans|construction-and-.lead: Larger amounts over longer terms for contractors with property to offer, such as a yard, a workshop or a director’s investment property.
intro: Many established trade businesses have property somewhere: a yard with a workshop, a unit, or a buy-to-let owned by a director. A secured loan puts a charge over that property and lets the company borrow more, for longer, than its trading record alone would justify. For a contractor wanting to buy a competitor, take on a major framework contract or move into a larger site, the extra scale matters, as these needs are often beyond what unsecured lenders will fund.

Construction trading figures are also less steady than some sectors, with profit swinging between years as jobs start and finish. Security evens this out for the lender, which is why secured loans can be available when a lender might be cautious about a profitable but lumpy year. The amount is driven by the property value and any existing borrowing, with the trading and order book used to show that repayments are affordable.
uses: Buying a competitor
Acquire a smaller firm or its contracts, with the loan sized to include the price, plant and a working capital cushion.
Moving to a larger yard
Buy or improve a depot with room for plant and storage, where the property itself adds to the security.
Taking on framework work
Prepare for a multi-year contract by buying plant, hiring staff and building up materials before the first payments arrive.
Refinancing expensive debt
Replace shorter or costlier borrowing, such as merchant advances, with a longer loan that costs less each month.
fit: Amounts and terms

Secured loans can range from £50,000 to several million, and terms often run from three to twenty years. As an illustration, a firm with a £600,000 yard and £250,000 outstanding might find up to £150,000 of further borrowing possible, subject to the lender’s valuation and checks.
Which property can be used

Commercial property is common, but lenders also consider residential investment property or, with care, a director’s home. Each lender has its own view on property type and location, and some will not lend on certain constructions or flood-risk areas.
What lenders check

A valuation, legal title, the company’s accounts and order book, and the directors’ finances. They may ask about work in hand, key customers and contract terms, because construction profit can be uneven. Expect the process to take several weeks.
considerations: Property at risk

If repayments are missed the lender can take action over the property, which may be a business asset or a director’s own. Understand the exact terms and take legal advice before you offer personal property.
Fees and delays

Valuations, legal fees and arrangement fees add to the cost, and the process is slower than unsecured lending. If you need the money quickly, a bridging loan or an unsecured loan may be considered first.
Over-borrowing in good years
A strong year can tempt a firm to borrow at its limit. Construction downturns can be sharp, so borrow an amount the business can repay in a poor year, not only in the best one.
faqs: Can I use a director’s buy-to-let as security?

Often yes, subject to the lender’s valuation and any mortgage already on it. The property owner would normally need to agree and take independent legal advice, since their own asset is on the line. If the property has a mortgage, the first lender’s consent may be needed.
What is the difference from asset finance?

Asset finance is secured on the specific machine or vehicle being bought. A secured loan is secured on property and can be used more widely, such as for working capital or an acquisition. A broker can say which fits your plan.
Will a debenture be required?

Some lenders take a debenture, a charge over the company’s assets, as well as the property. This gives them wider security and can mean other lenders are less willing to provide finance, so ask what is being asked for. Ask whether the debenture will be released when the loan is repaid, and how quickly.
Does the order book matter?

Yes, particularly for larger loans. Lenders like to see signed contracts and consistent work, as it supports repayment. Prepare a summary of your current jobs, customers and expected income. Include customer names, contract values and expected completion dates, as lenders may contact customers to verify them.
Can I borrow if a project is delayed?

Existing loans remain due. If you already hold a secured loan and a project is delayed, speak to the lender early. For new borrowing, lenders may be cautious if work has stalled, so be open with the broker. Early notice of a delay is usually better received than a surprise, and may lead to useful flexibility on terms.

bridging-loans|construction-and-trades.h1: Bridging loans for construction and trades
bridging-loans|construction-and-trades.title: Bridging Loans for Builders and Developers | Loanleaf
bridging-loans|construction-and-trades.desc: How bridging loans work for UK builders and contractors buying property to refurbish, at auction or between contracts. Free introduction to a broker.
bridging-loans|construction-and-trades.lead: Short-term finance secured on property, for builders buying to refurbish, completing an auction purchase or waiting on a sale.
intro: Builders often meet property finance from the other side: they buy a run-down house or commercial unit, renovate it and sell or refinance. A bridging loan fits that rhythm. It is short-term finance, secured on the property, with a term from a few weeks to around a year or two, and it can be arranged faster than most mortgages. That matters at auction, where completion is usually required within 28 days, or when a vendor wants a quick, certain buyer.

Lenders focus on the property and the plan for repaying the loan, called the exit. For a refurbishment, that is usually a sale or a refinance onto longer-term finance once works are done. Some lenders release the money in stages as work is completed. They will want a realistic budget, a programme and evidence the contractor, which may be your own firm, has done similar work. Interest is often rolled up into the loan, so the balance grows through the term.
uses: Auction purchases
Complete within the auction deadline, then refinance or sell once the property is let or renovated.
Buy, refurbish, sell
Fund a purchase and works on a property that a standard mortgage lender would not touch in its current condition.
Waiting for a sale
Release cash from one property while the sale of another is still in progress, so you can start the next project.
Planning-led projects
Cover the cost of a site while planning permission is sought, with the exit being a sale or development finance.
fit: Amounts and loan-to-value

Lenders often lend up to around 65% to 75% of a property’s value, with some offering more on a gross basis against the finished value, depending on the project. For example, a £250,000 house needing £50,000 of works might support a loan of £150,000 to £190,000, subject to valuation.
Short terms and higher cost

Bridging usually costs more than a standard mortgage, and fees can include arrangement, valuation, legal and exit charges. It is designed to be repaid within a short time, not held for years, so the exit plan sets the real cost.
What lenders check

The property’s value, its condition, your experience, the works budget and the exit route. A track record of completed projects helps. Because the loan is secured on property, a personal guarantee is common, so understand how it works before agreeing.
considerations: Exit risk
If a sale falls through or works overrun, the loan may need extending at extra cost, and in a poor case the lender can enforce against the property. Add contingency to your programme and budget.
Not for working capital

Bridging is secured on property and priced for short periods. Using it to cover wages or materials on a general contract is expensive and risky, and an unsecured loan, invoice finance or a facility is likely to suit better.
Cost of delays
Interest runs every month, so a three-month overrun can add several percent to the total. Check monthly rates, fees and whether there are charges for early or late repayment.
faqs: How quickly can a bridging loan complete?

Faster than most mortgages, sometimes in a couple of weeks when documents and the valuation are in place. Auction purchases usually need a broker to start early, since the deadline is fixed. Valuations and legal work are usually what set the pace, so appoint a solicitor who knows bridging.
Can I get bridging on a property that is not habitable?

Often yes, which is a main reason builders use it. Lenders will look at the property’s condition, the works plan and the exit. Some release money in stages as work progresses. Where works are substantial, lenders may ask for a schedule of works and a builder’s quote before they agree terms.
Do I need to own the property already?

No. Bridging can fund a purchase. Lenders will normally also consider your experience and what you are putting in as a deposit, which is often 25% to 35% of the price. Your experience of similar projects, and a clear plan for the exit, matter as much as the deposit.
What happens at the end of the term?

The loan and any rolled-up interest must be repaid, usually from a sale or refinance. If this is not possible, you would need to agree an extension or other plan with the lender, and costs may rise. Agreeing an extension before the term ends is usually easier than negotiating after it has expired.
Can a limited company take a bridging loan?

Yes, and many borrowers are companies, often special purpose vehicles. Lenders will assess the company and may ask directors for personal guarantees. Loanleaf works with companies trading for six months or more with revenue of at least £50,000. Where several companies are involved, the broker will need to know how they are linked.

vat-and-tax-loans|construction-and-trade.h1: VAT and tax loans for construction and trades
vat-and-tax-loans|construction-and-trade.title: VAT and Tax Loans for Construction and Trades | Loanleaf
vat-and-tax-loans|construction-and-trade.desc: How VAT and tax loans work for UK builders and trade firms facing VAT, PAYE or corporation tax bills before customer payments arrive. Free broker match.
vat-and-tax-loans|construction-and-trade.lead: Pay HMRC on time while you wait for stage payments and retentions, and spread the cost across a few months.
intro: Construction businesses can owe tax on money they have not yet received. VAT may be due on an invoice that is still 60 days from being paid, and PAYE and National Insurance on wages fall due every month regardless. Corporation tax arrives nine months after year end, often just when retentions are still tied up and plant needs replacing. The result is a company that is profitable on paper but short of cash on the day HMRC expects payment.

A tax loan is a short-term loan used to pay the bill and then repaid in fixed instalments over a few months. It does not reduce the amount owed, but it avoids late-payment penalties and interest, and keeps working capital free for materials and wages. Lenders will check that returns are filed, that the company is profitable and that no arrears are already building up. Having the VAT return or tax computation to hand helps the broker move quickly.
uses: Quarterly VAT on unpaid invoices
Settle the VAT due on work you have billed but not yet been paid for, then repay from the receipts that follow.
PAYE and CIS-related payments
Meet employer tax payments during a stretch with fewer billable jobs, without delaying wages.
Corporation tax after a strong year
Pay a large bill from profit that is already invested in plant, stock or a second crew.
Retention-heavy completion
Bridge the tax cost of a finished job whose retentions will not release for twelve months.
fit: Terms and amounts

Terms are often between three and twelve months. A contractor facing a £45,000 VAT bill might, for example, repay it over six months, subject to checks, and need to budget for the monthly amount on top of fees. The lender may pay HMRC directly or release money to the company.
Domestic reverse charge and cash timing

Under the domestic reverse charge, many subcontract invoices carry no VAT collected, while main contractors account for it. This changes the size and timing of bills, so check your VAT position with your accountant and use your latest return as the basis for borrowing.
What lenders check

Up-to-date filings, profitability, and a clean tax record. They also check bank statements for signs of cash strain. If there are arrears or a Time to Pay arrangement already, fewer lenders will consider it, so raise that with the broker at the start.
considerations: Compare with Time to Pay
HMRC may agree to spread a bill, charging interest on the balance. A loan has its own interest and fees but gives certainty. Work out the total cost of each before choosing.
Don’t borrow to avoid a deeper problem
If payments to HMRC are routinely hard to meet, a loan may only delay the issue. Speak to your accountant about how the business sets money aside, and review your payment terms and pricing.
Time pressure
Applications take time, so approach a broker as soon as you can see the bill coming. A late payment can lead to penalties and interest from HMRC, which add to the cost.
faqs: Can a loan pay my CIS tax liabilities?

Lenders usually focus on VAT, PAYE or corporation tax bills. If your concern is CIS deductions made by contractors, these are credited against your tax, so ask the broker which bills a lender will accept as the purpose. Mention any CIS refunds you expect, since they affect how the lender sees your cash position.
Does HMRC need to know about the loan?

No, the loan is between your company and the lender. If the lender pays HMRC directly, HMRC will see a payment on your account in the usual way. You do not need HMRC’s permission, though you should still file your return and pay on time.
How fast can this be arranged?

Faster than many loans because the amount and purpose are clear, though still subject to the lender’s checks. Allow plenty of time before the deadline and have the return or demand ready. If a payment date is close, tell the broker straight away, as some lenders can move faster than others.
Will it affect my ability to get other finance?

It adds a monthly commitment, which other lenders will take into account. A short term clears quickly, so the effect on future applications is often brief. Lenders mainly look at whether you have repaid previous borrowing on time, which a clean record on a short loan can support.
Is there a minimum size?

Loanleaf handles enquiries from £5,000. Lenders set their own minimums for tax loans, and larger bills may have more options. The broker can say which lenders suit your bill. Smaller bills may have fewer lenders interested, so a broker may suggest a different route.

revolving-credit-facility|retail.title: Revolving Credit Facility for Retailers | Loanleaf
revolving-credit-facility|retail.desc: How a revolving credit facility helps UK shops and online retailers buy stock ahead of peak trading and manage the gaps in between. Free broker introduction.
revolving-credit-facility|retail.lead: A credit limit for buying stock ahead of a peak, repaid as the stock sells, with interest only on what you use.
intro: A retailer’s biggest costs come before its biggest sales. Christmas stock is ordered in the summer, spring ranges in the winter, and suppliers often want payment on order or within a few weeks. Meanwhile rent, rates and wages keep falling due. A revolving credit facility offers a limit agreed in advance, which you draw down to place the order and repay as the stock sells through. Once repaid, the headroom is available again for the next buy.

The pattern of the facility is a good fit for stock cycles: balance up in the autumn, down in January. Because interest is charged only on what you use, a facility can cost less than a loan taken for a short period, although arrangement fees apply and the lender may review the limit yearly. Lenders look at turnover, margin and stock levels, and may take a charge over stock or company assets. A broker can say which lenders understand retail.
uses: Buying ahead of Christmas
Place a large autumn order with suppliers to get better prices or secure scarce lines, repaying from December and January sales.
Seasonal ranges
Fund summer or back-to-school stock that arrives months before customers start buying.
Taking up a supplier discount
Pay a manufacturer early for a bulk-buy discount where the saving outweighs the interest cost.
Smoothing weak weeks
Cover rent and wages through a quiet month, such as January or after a poor trading period, without a fresh loan application.
fit: Limits and stock

Lenders often size the limit from turnover and the pattern of cash in your account, and some consider the value of stock. A shop with £1.2m turnover might be offered a limit in the tens of thousands or more, subject to checks. Ask for a limit that covers your peak buy, not the most on offer.
Matching the cycle

The facility should be near its limit around the time stock arrives and clear after your busiest period. If the balance stays high through the year, the lender may see the business as needing a loan. Plan repayments around known trading peaks.
What lenders check

Bank statements, accounts, margin trends and how fast stock turns. A retailer with slow-moving lines or heavy markdowns may be treated more cautiously. Online and in-store sales can be shown separately, which helps lenders understand the mix.
considerations: Stock that doesn’t sell
If a range fails, the facility stays drawn while the stock sits in the stockroom. Keep the amount you draw in line with what you realistically expect to sell, and leave a margin.
Variable cost and fees
Interest and fees vary, and the cost of keeping a balance drawn for months can exceed a fixed-term loan. Add up the likely cost across a full cycle before deciding.
Reviews and security
Limits are normally reviewed, often yearly, and a lender may reduce the limit if trading weakens. Some facilities are secured against stock or have director guarantees, so read the terms carefully.
faqs: Can I use a facility to pay overseas suppliers?

Generally yes, as the money is a general business facility. Currency risk is yours, so think about how exchange rates could affect the cost of the stock. Some lenders offer separate trade finance for imports, which a broker can explain.
Is it better than a loan for stock?

For repeated, short-term buying it can be, because you pay interest only when drawn. For a one-off larger purchase, a fixed-term loan may be simpler. A broker can compare for your pattern of trading. A mix is sometimes used, with a facility for regular stock and a loan for a refit.
What if sales are lower than planned?

The facility remains due. If stock sells slowly, you may need to repay from other cash or ask the lender to extend. Talk to the broker about a limit and terms you can handle in a weak season. Telling the lender early, before a limit review, usually leads to a better outcome.
Will the lender take security over my stock?

Some do, by taking a charge over company assets, and others do not. Stock is hard to value, so lenders tend to rely on turnover and cash flow, particularly for smaller facilities. Where a charge is taken, the lender may ask for stock lists and insurance details.
Can an online retailer use this?

Yes. Lenders look at your bank account and platform sales, and may ask for marketplace statements. Online businesses often have clear data, which can help the assessment. Having clear records of returns and refunds, which are common in online retail, supports the application.

merchant-cash-advance|retail.title: Merchant Cash Advance for Retailers | Loanleaf
merchant-cash-advance|retail.desc: How a merchant cash advance works for UK shops and online retailers, with repayments taken as a share of card and online sales. Free broker introduction.
merchant-cash-advance|retail.lead: An advance repaid from a share of card and online sales, so repayments follow footfall and basket size through the year.
intro: Shops take most of their money through a card terminal or a payment processor, and that history is what a merchant cash advance provider assesses. If your terminal has recorded six to twelve months of steady sales, a provider can offer an advance based on its volume, even if the company has few assets and a short track record. A share of each day’s card sales then goes towards repaying the advance, until the agreed total is cleared.

For retailers this can mean repayments that rise around payday weekends and sale periods and ease in dull weeks. Some providers also include online sales through a payment processor, though not all do, and marketplace payouts, cash and bank transfers may be excluded.
