Since the cost is a fixed fee rather than an annual rate, it can be hard to compare with a loan, so it helps to ask for the total repayable and the expected time to clear.
uses: Last-minute stock
Buy extra stock when a line is selling faster than planned, or when a supplier offers a one-off deal.
Refreshing the shop
Pay for shelving, lighting or a new till system without agreeing to fixed monthly payments.
Marketing around a sale
Fund advertising ahead of Black Friday or a seasonal sale, with repayments scaled by the extra sales it brings.
Cover for a slow patch
Pay rent and wages in a quiet month and let the repayment share fall with takings.
fit: How an advance is sized

Providers often offer a multiple of average monthly card takings, so a shop taking £30,000 a month on the terminal might be offered a few months’ worth, subject to checks. The advance is repaid within a period that depends on sales, though many providers expect a target timeframe.
Card, online and cash mix

The more of your trade passes through the terminal or processor, the more the provider can see and the easier the assessment. Retailers with a large cash share, or with most sales on a third-party marketplace, may find the amount lower.
What providers check

Card turnover history, consistency, refunds and chargebacks, and the terminal provider. A change of provider mid-advance usually needs agreement. Some providers also ask for bank statements or a director’s guarantee.
considerations: The effective cost
A fixed fee can be a high annual cost if the advance is repaid in a few months. Compare the total repayable with an unsecured loan or a facility, and think about what the money will earn.
Takings reduced every day
A share of each sale is taken before it reaches the bank, which can pinch cash for rent and supplier payments. Work out your remaining takings after the share and check they cover costs.
Not for large investments
Advances are best for smaller, quick needs. A major refit or a new branch is likely to suit a fixed-term loan better, with a repayment schedule you can plan for.
faqs: Do Shopify or other online sales count?

Some providers take online payment processor volume into account, while others focus only on in-store terminals. Tell the broker how your sales split between channels so they can approach suitable providers. Some also accept data from payment providers such as Stripe or PayPal, so ask which are recognised.
What if my returns rate is high?

Providers look at net takings, and a high rate of refunds or chargebacks may reduce the advance. Showing that returns are normal for your product type helps. Provide recent months of terminal reports, as this shows the pattern more clearly than a summary.
Can I repay the advance early?

Often yes, but because the cost is a fixed fee, early repayment may not reduce it much. Check whether any discount is available, and ask what the total payable is if you clear it in half the expected time. Some providers allow part-repayment or renewal once a set share has been repaid, which can change the cost.
Is a merchant cash advance regulated?

Advances to companies are generally not regulated by the FCA, so some protections do not apply. Read the agreement closely, particularly the terms on switching terminals, closure and default. Ask a solicitor to read the agreement if the sum is large, particularly clauses about default and guarantees.
Does it affect my ability to get other finance?

Other lenders will see the share of takings going to the provider and may treat it as a commitment. It can limit the amount you can borrow elsewhere until it is repaid. Some lenders will wait until the advance is mostly repaid, which a broker can plan around.

unsecured-business-loans|retail.title: Unsecured Business Loans for Retailers | Loanleaf
unsecured-business-loans|retail.desc: How unsecured business loans work for UK shops and online retailers paying for a refit, a new branch or a till and website upgrade. Free broker match.
unsecured-business-loans|retail.lead: A fixed sum for a refit, a new branch or a systems upgrade, repaid monthly without offering property or stock as security.
intro: Most one-off retail projects are really about the next five years of trading: a shopfront and layout that keeps customers walking in, a new till and stock system that reduces errors, or a second branch in a nearby town. An unsecured loan funds such a project as a single sum, repaid in fixed instalments, without a charge over your stock or lease. Lenders judge the application on the company’s trading record and on whether the extra income from the project can cover the repayment.

The term should be matched to the benefit. Fixtures and fittings that last six or seven years can reasonably be spread over three to five, while stock bought for a season should be repaid within a few months. Lenders usually ask for a year of bank statements so they can see how the shop trades through peaks and troughs. A broker can build the application around a clear plan, which tends to help.
uses: Shopfit and refresh
Replace flooring, lighting and displays to refresh a store that is looking tired, paying the contractor on completion.
New branch or pop-up
Cover the deposit, fit-out and opening stock for a second location once the first is trading well.
Systems and website
Buy a new EPOS, stock management system or ecommerce build that reduces costs and supports growth.
Larger one-off stock buy
Purchase a bulk order at a discount, when the saving more than covers the cost of borrowing.
fit: Typical sums and terms

Loans from £5,000 to several hundred thousand are possible, with terms of one to five years. A gift shop with £400,000 in sales might, for example, borrow £30,000 for a refit over three years, subject to lender checks. Longer terms reduce the payment but add to the total interest.
Showing the return

Lenders respond well to a simple case: quotes for the work, an estimate of the extra sales and a statement of how repayments fit within the existing figures. Weak margins or falling sales make it harder, so be ready to explain the trend.
What lenders check

Bank statements, filed accounts, existing borrowing and credit history for the company and directors. Lease length matters for retailers who rent their shop, as a short remaining lease can reduce the amount or term offered.
considerations: Personal guarantees
Directors are usually asked to guarantee unsecured loans. For a small retailer, that is a real personal commitment if sales fall.
Fixed payments against changeable footfall
A fixed repayment must be met whether the high street is busy or not. Test the figure against your weakest month over the past year.
Cost compared with asset finance
If the purchase is equipment such as shelving or refrigeration, asset finance may cost less since the kit is the security. A broker can say whether that applies to your project.
faqs: Can I get a loan if I rent my shop?

Yes. Unsecured lending does not rely on owning property. Lenders may ask about the lease, since it supports the business’s future at the location, so share the remaining term and any renewal plans. A lease with several years left, or a recent renewal, generally makes the application stronger.
Will it matter if I sell mostly online?

Online retailers are routinely assessed on bank statements and platform data. Marketplace sellers should expect lenders to ask about dependence on one platform and what would happen if it changed its rules. Show platform fees and returns clearly in your accounts so the lender can see your true margin.
How much can a retailer usually borrow?

It depends on turnover, profit and existing commitments. Lenders often base limits on a share of annual revenue, and a broker can give a realistic range once they have seen your accounts. Larger amounts usually need stronger profit, so the broker may suggest phasing a bigger project.
Can I use the loan for stock?

Many lenders allow it, though the term should match the stock’s selling period. For regular stock buying across the year, a revolving facility may be a better fit than a fixed-term loan. If you buy stock several times a year, explore the facility option with the broker.
How long does it take?

Some lenders decide within days, but larger sums take longer. Having bank statements, accounts and any quotes ready tends to speed things up. Gaps in your documents are the most common cause of delay, so check them before you apply.

asset-finance|retail.title: Asset Finance for Shops and Retailers | Loanleaf
asset-finance|retail.desc: How asset finance works for UK shops and retailers buying EPOS systems, refrigeration, delivery vans and warehouse kit. Free match with a specialist broker.
asset-finance|retail.lead: Spread the cost of tills, chillers, shelving and delivery vans over their useful life, with the equipment as security.
intro: A shop contains a surprising amount of financeable kit: refrigerated displays and chillers, EPOS hardware, security systems, a delivery van, racking in the stockroom or warehouse, and for larger retailers, forklifts and packing equipment. Asset finance lets the company pay for these in instalments, with the lender holding the equipment as security. It leaves the company’s bank limits and cash free for stock, which is where most retail money is needed.

Not everything holds its value. A refrigerated cabinet or a van is easy to resell, so lenders treat it well. Bespoke shopfittings, signage and software bolted into the premises are hard to recover and may not qualify. Technology also loses value fast, so lenders often prefer shorter terms for tills and tablets. A broker can help split a quote into items lenders will finance and items that need another source.
uses: Chillers and freezers
Finance refrigerated units for a convenience or food shop, spreading the cost across the years they will run.
EPOS and stock systems
Pay for tills, scanners and software on a lease, often with support included, rather than a large one-off bill.
Delivery vans and cargo bikes
Add a vehicle for local delivery or click-and-collect without taking cash from stock purchasing.
Warehouse and packing kit
Buy racking, conveyors or a forklift when online orders outgrow the stockroom.
fit: Terms by asset type

Vehicles and refrigeration may be financed over three to five years, while EPOS and computers are often leased over two to three because they date quickly. A shop spending £18,000 on chillers and tills, for example, might split the term between the two, subject to lender checks.
Hire purchase or lease

Hire purchase suits assets you will use for their full life. Leasing keeps monthly cost lower and can allow upgrades, which suits technology. Accounting, VAT and tax treatment differ, so take your accountant’s view before choosing.
What lenders check

A supplier quote, the type and age of the asset, and your accounts and statements. Used equipment from a dealer is usually easier than a private sale. If you rent your shop, lenders may ask about the lease because equipment must stay accessible.
considerations: Technology moves on
A till system financed over five years may be outdated well before the end. Choose a shorter term or lease with upgrade options, and check what happens if the supplier stops supporting the software.
Fixed payments, changing footfall
Payments continue whatever the footfall does. Check the monthly cost against your weakest months and avoid spreading too many items across overlapping agreements.
Items that won’t qualify
Signage, decoration and installation labour are often excluded. Ask the supplier to itemise the quote and plan another way to cover the rest, such as an unsecured loan or cash.
faqs: Can I finance a shopfit?

Usually only the movable, resaleable parts such as units and refrigeration. Built-in joinery, decoration and labour are harder to finance, so a loan may be needed alongside asset finance. Ask your fitter to list each item separately, so the lender can see what can be recovered and resold.
Is software financeable?

Some lenders will include software bundled with hardware, such as an EPOS system, though standalone software and subscriptions are harder. Ask the supplier how the quote is structured. Subscription fees for ongoing support are usually paid separately and sit outside the finance agreement.
What if I move shop?

Fixed items may be affected, and the lender may need to know where the asset is. Tell the lender if you are planning a move and ask about their conditions on location. Kit that can be moved is easier to deal with, while fixed installations may need a separate agreement.
Can a new retailer get asset finance?

Loanleaf works with businesses trading six months or more with revenue of at least £50,000. A younger company may be asked for a larger deposit or a guarantee, depending on the lender. Strong sales since opening and a clear supplier quote help show the purchase is affordable.
Is a deposit always needed?

Not always. Some lenders finance the full price for established businesses, while others ask for a deposit, especially for used items or newer companies. The broker can explain what to expect. A deposit can lower the monthly payment, though it takes cash from stock, so weigh both.

vat-and-tax-loans|retail.h1: VAT and tax loans for retail
vat-and-tax-loans|retail.title: VAT and Tax Loans for Retailers | Loanleaf
vat-and-tax-loans|retail.desc: How VAT and tax loans work for UK shops and online retailers when a VAT bill lands after cash has gone into stock. Free match with a specialist finance broker.
vat-and-tax-loans|retail.lead: Pay a VAT or corporation tax bill on time when your cash is sitting on the shelves as stock, and repay over a few months.
intro: Retailers collect VAT on most sales, and the quarterly bill is a share of everything sold, but their cash is often tied up elsewhere. After Christmas, many shops have taken large VAT-inclusive sales while spending the money on January’s stock, rent and rates. The VAT is due about five weeks after the quarter ends, and by then the cash that came in during December has often been spent. A tax loan lets the company pay HMRC on time and repay the lender in instalments.

The loan is for a known bill, so assessment is more focused than for a general loan. Lenders look for a profitable business, returns filed on time and no existing arrears. They will usually ask for the VAT return showing the amount and due date, plus a few months of bank statements. A retailer with a clean record and a one-off bill is easier to assess than one who regularly pays late.
uses: VAT after peak trading
Pay the quarter’s VAT after a busy November and December, before January sales bring cash back in.
Corporation tax after a good year
Settle a large bill while profit is already committed to stock and a refit.
PAYE and NI in a quiet spell
Meet employment taxes for a larger team through the weeks after seasonal staff have been taken on.
Import-related VAT
Cover VAT on a large import shipment, where the tax is due before the goods are on sale.
fit: Amounts and terms

Tax loans usually run from three to twelve months. A shop facing a £28,000 VAT bill might, for example, repay it over six months, subject to checks, with a fee on top. Because the term is short, the monthly repayment is larger than for a longer loan of the same size.
Retail VAT schemes

Some retailers use special VAT schemes, which change how the bill is calculated and when it is due. Your accountant can confirm the amount and timing, and having these figures to hand helps the broker approach lenders accurately.
Compared with other options

If the need is regular, such as every quarter, a revolving facility may serve better. If stock is the cause, asset-light finance against stock or a merchant advance based on sales could help. A tax loan fits a one-off bill with a clear repayment plan.
considerations: It does not cut the bill
A tax loan only spreads the cost. Make sure the extra monthly repayment still fits alongside stock buying and rent, and plan for the next quarter’s VAT as well.
Timing risk
Applications take days or weeks, and a late payment brings HMRC interest and penalties. Start well before the due date, and have your return and statements ready.
Cost compared with Time to Pay
HMRC may agree a Time to Pay arrangement, charging interest on the balance. A loan costs differently and brings fees. Compare the two for your own figures.
faqs: Can I borrow if I have a Time to Pay arrangement?

Fewer lenders will consider it, though some may if payments are up to date. A broker can say which lenders would look at your situation. Keeping every Time to Pay instalment up to date is the most important thing for a lender reviewing your case.
Does the loan clear VAT on imports?

Some lenders will fund import VAT as a tax bill, others may treat it as general borrowing. Tell the broker about the import schedule and how much VAT is due. Postponed VAT accounting can change when the bill is due, so check the timing with your accountant.
Will online sales affect the assessment?

Not particularly. Lenders look at overall profitability and the VAT return. Marketplace sellers should have clean records of platform fees and payouts so the figures reconcile. Overseas sales and different VAT rules can complicate the figures, so your accountant’s summary will help.
Is the loan paid straight to HMRC?

Sometimes. Some lenders pay HMRC directly and others pay the company to settle the bill. Either way, you remain responsible for making sure HMRC receives the payment by the deadline. Some lenders ask for the payment reference or demand to confirm the money is used for the stated bill.
What if my VAT bill is much bigger than usual?

Lenders will want to understand why, such as a big import or a strong quarter. Be ready with an explanation and supporting figures. It helps the lender to see the bill is expected rather than a sign of stress. If it relates to a one-off event, such as a big import, a clear note from your accountant can help.

commercial-mortgages|retail.title: Commercial Mortgages for Shops and Retailers | Loanleaf
commercial-mortgages|retail.desc: How commercial mortgages work for UK retailers buying their shop, refinancing premises or buying an investment unit. Free introduction to a specialist broker.
commercial-mortgages|retail.lead: Long-term finance to buy or refinance the shop you trade from, valued on location, tenure and what the unit could let for.
intro: Retailers who rent often spend years paying a landlord for a unit they could own, and a commercial mortgage is how many make the change. The lender lends against the property, usually up to around 65% to 75% of its value, over fifteen to twenty-five years. Repayments on a shop you occupy yourself can sit close to the rent you pay, while the capital is building up as equity. The lender cares about the building and the business that will pay for it.

Retail property is valued with care, because shops vary widely. A unit on a busy high street, a retail park unit and a village corner shop attract different lenders, and a unit with a flat above, or vacant possession, changes the picture. Lenders will look at the location, the lease history if any, the unit’s condition and whether the shop could be re-let or sold if the business ever closed. A broker can match your property type with lenders who are comfortable with it.
uses: Buying your own shop
Purchase the unit you currently rent, so payments build equity and you are no longer exposed to rent reviews.
Refinancing premises
Replace an expensive short-term loan on a shop you already own with a longer-term mortgage that reduces monthly outgoings.
Releasing equity
Borrow against a shop you own to pay for stock, a refit or a second branch.
Buying an investment unit
Purchase a shop to let to another tenant, with the rent covering much of the repayment.
fit: Deposits and terms

Expect a deposit of 25% to 35% of the price, plus valuation and legal fees. A £400,000 shop might need around £100,000 to £140,000 up front, subject to lender checks. Terms of fifteen to twenty-five years are common, with fixed or variable rates.
Owner-occupier or investment

If you will trade from the property, lenders assess the retail business’s profit and its ability to cover repayments. If you will let it, they usually look at the rental income, and a tenant on a long lease with a strong covenant helps.
What lenders check

A valuation, title, planning use class, the condition of the building and, for owner-occupiers, two to three years of accounts. Properties with short leases, in decline or with unusual use may limit options, so be ready to explain.
considerations: High streets change
Retail property values and demand vary by location and can move over a long loan term. A lender may take a cautious view of secondary locations, which affects the amount and the rate.
Costs and time
Valuation, legal and arrangement fees add to the deposit, and the process takes weeks. Budget for these and for maintenance, insurance and business rates, which come with ownership.
Tying up capital
A deposit spent on property is money not available for stock. Make sure the business keeps enough working capital, or consider a revolving facility alongside the mortgage.
faqs: Can I buy a shop with a flat above?

Often, and some lenders prefer mixed-use property. The valuation will cover both parts, and whether you live in the flat or let it affects the type of mortgage and the lenders available. If the flat is let on a tenancy, the lender may ask to see the agreement and the rent being paid.
Do lenders prefer prime high streets?

Many do, but some will lend on secondary locations, parades and local shops at lower loan-to-value. A broker can say which lenders accept your type of unit. Expect a lower loan-to-value and a higher rate for weaker locations, since resale and letting are harder.
Is the shop’s existing lease a problem?

If you are buying the property you occupy, the lease ends. If you are buying an investment unit with a tenant in place, lenders will check the lease length, rent and tenant’s strength. If a tenant has a right to renew, the lender will also want to understand how that affects value.
Can a retailer with a short history get a commercial mortgage?

Loanleaf works with companies trading six months or more and with at least £50,000 of annual revenue, but mortgage lenders often want longer accounts. A larger deposit may help, and a broker can say which lenders are flexible. Management accounts and a clear business plan can help where filed accounts are short.
What if I want to buy at auction?

Auction purchases usually need to complete within 28 days, which is quicker than a mortgage can arrive. A bridging loan may be used first and then refinanced onto a commercial mortgage. Plan the exit onto a mortgage before you commit, since the valuation may differ from the price you paid.
